# Diagnosing a Peugeot 307: Buzzing Noise, No Crank, and Stuck Emission Light

When a vehicle makes a constant buzzing noise from under the bonnet upon turning the key to the start position but refuses to crank, you are almost certainly witnessing an electrical relay or starter solenoid in distress. In the context of your Peugeot 307, this symptom is distinct from a dead battery because all electricsâincluding lights and the stereoâfunction normally when the ignition is set to "ON." This isolation confirms that the alternator is likely charging the system correctly and that there is sufficient voltage present at the battery terminals. The issue lies specifically in the high-current path required to engage the starter motor.

The buzzing sound you hear is the electromagnetic coil of the starter solenoid attempting to pull the plunger into place but failing due to insufficient torque or a mechanical obstruction. This often happens when the starter motor's internal brushes are worn out, or the pinion gear fails to mesh properly with the flywheel ring gear. Since the car ran fine this morning and is now stuck, the failure mode has likely progressed from an intermittent electrical connection to a complete mechanical seizure or a total depletion of the battery's reserve capacity under load. Even though the battery is only 12 months old, lead-acid batteries can suffer from sulfation if left in a discharged state for too long, effectively rendering them unable to deliver the hundreds of amps needed for cranking despite showing good voltage on a multimeter.

A critical observation in your situation is the behavior of the emissions light (Check Engine Light). The fact that this light was off during the successful push start but is now constantly illuminated suggests the engine control unit (ECU) has detected a fault code related to the crankshaft position sensor or the starter circuit itself. Modern ECUs monitor the ignition cycle; if they do not see the expected voltage drop associated with the starter engaging, or if the crankshaft does not begin to rotate within a specific timeframe after the solenoid activates, they log a "no crank" fault and illuminate the warning light. This is why the car won't start again even though the battery has been recharged by the push start attempt.

Given that you cannot afford a garage visit, your immediate diagnostic steps must focus on isolating whether the failure is electrical (battery voltage under load) or mechanical (starter assembly). You can perform a simple voltage drop test using a multimeter. Connect the red probe to the positive battery terminal and the black probe to the starter motor's main power cable (usually thick and bolted directly to the battery via a fuse or relay). If you observe more than 0.5 volts while attempting to start, you have excessive resistance in your grounding strap or cables, which causes that buzzing sound as the system fights against the voltage drop.

If the wiring checks out, the starter motor assembly itself is likely faulty and requires replacement. This is a common wear item on the Peugeot 307 platform. While swapping the starter is a relatively straightforward mechanical job accessible from underneath the vehicle, it requires specific tools and knowledge of the car's suspension mounting points to create enough clearance. There is also the possibility of a failing ignition switch; if the internal contacts inside the "START" position are arcing or corroding, they may provide just enough power to light up the dashboard but not enough to fully energize the high-current starter solenoid.

Since you need the vehicle operational immediately for essential travel, consider contacting local independent mechanics who might offer a mobile service to swap the starter unit on-site. If the emissions light remains on after the repair, you will eventually need an OBDII scanner to clear the stored fault codes, but this is often secondary to physically restoring the cranking capability.
